D-DOIT: Training-free Adaptation of Discrete Diffusion via Doob’s h-Transform

Jieke Wu‡{}^{\>\;{\ddagger}},  Qijie Zhu*§,  Weimin Wu*†,  Zeqi Ye♮,  Minshuo Chen♮,  Han Liu†§
†{}^{\dagger}\;Center for Foundation Models and Generative AI, Northwestern University Department of Computer Science, Northwestern University ‡{}^{\ddagger}\;Department of Computer Science, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology §{}^{\lx@sectionsign}\;Department of Statistics and Data Science, Northwestern University ♮{}^{\natural}\;Industrial Engineering & Management Sciences, Northwestern University
jieke.wu@kaust.edu.sa, {qijiezhu2029,wwm,zeqiye2029}@u.northwestern.edu minshuo.chen@northwestern.edu, hanliu@northwestern.edu ††thanks: Equal contribution.
Abstract

We propose D-DOIT (Discrete Doob-Oriented Inference-time Transformation), a training-free and efficient adaptation method for discrete diffusion models with generic rewards. D-DOIT formulates adaptation as sampling from a reward-tilted target distribution and realizes this transport through Doob’s hh-transform of the discrete diffusion reverse kernel, using only reward values rather than reward gradients. Unlike continuous diffusion, masked discrete diffusion samples categorical token-reveal transitions rather than continuous state updates. D-DOIT derives the corresponding discrete Doob’s hh-transform, which guides sampling by reweighting reverse transition probabilities instead of adding a drift correction. To make this transformation practical, D-DOIT avoids expensive future rollouts. At each guided step, D-DOIT samples candidate next states, uses the model prediction head to complete each candidate into a clean sequence, evaluates each completion with the reward oracle, and resamples the next state with probabilities proportional to the rewards. An optional late-stage best-of-KK refinement further improves sample quality by branching trajectories only near the end of denoising, avoiding the KK-fold cost over the full trajectory. Empirically, across regulatory DNA design and protein inverse folding benchmarks, D-DOIT outperforms training-free guidance baselines. It improves enhancer activity and cell-type specificity while preserving sequence naturalness, and achieves the highest success rate in protein inverse folding.

Project Page: https://github.com/WeiminWu2000/D-DOIT.

1 Introduction

We propose D-DOIT (Discrete Doob-Oriented Inference-time Transformation), a training-free sampler for reward-guided masked discrete diffusion. Discrete diffusion has become a strong generative modeling paradigm for finite-vocabulary data [1, 2]. Masked discrete diffusion models are especially attractive for biological sequences because they predict clean tokens from partially masked states and provide tractable categorical reverse kernels [3, 4, 5]. These models have recently been used for DNA and protein generation [6, 7, 8], where the scientific objective is rarely just to sample from the pre-trained distribution. Instead, a practitioner usually wants sequences with high activity, specificity, or other task-level scores for sequence design.

Reward adaptation creates a tension between performance, generality, and cost. Training-based approaches can improve reward optimization, but they update the backbone and often require reward gradients, extra training, and hyperparameter tuning [8, 9]. Training-free methods keep the backbone fixed, but many either assume differentiable rewards or rely on particle and search procedures whose cost grows with trajectory history or search width [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17]. This motivates the question studied here: can a frozen masked diffusion model be adapted to generic black-box rewards by modifying only its inference-time sampling law?

Our starting point is to view adaptation as a distributional transport problem. Let pθp_{\theta} be the clean-sequence distribution induced by the frozen masked diffusion reverse chain, and let R:𝒳→ℝR:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} be a sequence-level reward. Rather than optimizing reward in isolation, we target the reward-tilted distribution πβ​(𝐱)∝pθ​(𝐱)​exp⁡(R⁡(𝐱)/β)\pi_{\beta}(\mathbf{x})\propto p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\exp(R(\bx)/\beta), which keeps the pre-trained model as a sequence prior while favoring high-reward outputs. Doob’s hh-transform gives the exact local transformation needed to sample from this tilted law. The central object is the downstream value h⁡(𝐱¯tl,tl)h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}},t_{l}), the expected terminal reward weight under the frozen reverse chain conditioned on the current partially denoised state.

The discrete setting changes how the transform must be implemented. In continuous diffusion, Doob guidance can be expressed as an additive score or drift correction [18, 19, 20, 21]. In masked discrete diffusion, the state space is categorical, generation proceeds through irreversible token-reveal transitions, and there is no Euclidean score field. D-DOIT therefore applies Doob’s hh-transform at the kernel level: each frozen reverse transition is multiplicatively reweighted by the downstream hh-value of the candidate next state. This yields a discrete analogue of the continuous Doob correction while preserving the frozen parameters and allowing black-box reward queries.

The exact transform still requires the future reward-to-go for every candidate reverse state, which is intractable by repeated rollouts. D-DOIT makes the transform executable with two approximations. First, it estimates candidate hh-values by using the masked diffusion prediction head to complete each candidate into a clean sequence, then evaluating the reward oracle on that completion. Second, it draws a finite set of candidate reverse states and selects among them with Doob-weighted probabilities. An optional best-of-KK refinement branches only after a chosen split update, which hedges irreversible token reveals without multiplying the full denoising trajectory cost. The same sampler gives two operating points: D-DOIT-LBOK-S for a lower-budget regime and D-DOIT-Q for high-budget quality evidence.

We evaluate D-DOIT on regulatory DNA sequence design and protein inverse folding. On the DRAKES HepG2 enhancer benchmark, the near-TDS-speed D-DOIT-LBOK-S matches TDS on predicted activity while substantially improving accessibility, 3-mer correlation, and motif correlation. The high-budget D-DOIT-Q setting reaches 6.196.19 predicted activity and exceeds training-based DRAKES on Pred-Activity, 3-mer Corr, and JASPAR Corr, while remaining slightly lower on ATAC-Acc. At a similar wall-clock budget, D-DOIT-Q also improves activity, accessibility, and 3-mer correlation over soft value-based decoding (SVDD-PM) and wall-clock-matched endpoint search. Endpoint search achieves higher JASPAR correlation. On the Ctrl-DNA cell-type-specific enhancer benchmark, D-DOIT is a clear training-free method that moves the specificity reward. D-DOIT-Q raises Δ​R\Delta R to 0.1190.119, with a trade-off in motif preservation, and D-DOIT-LBOK-S provides a lower-budget positive-reward point. At a matched wall-clock budget, however, endpoint search captures much of this gain, so the margin is smaller than on HepG2. Guidance with alternative predictors and transfer to held-out evaluators retain the gains over unguided sampling. On protein inverse folding, the same frozen backbone reaches 68.1%68.1\% joint stability–structure success. These results support D-DOIT as a training-free mechanism for reward-guided sequence generation, not as a matched-cost replacement for every high-budget or training-based method.

In summary, we make three contributions:

  • •

    Discrete Doob hh-transform for masked diffusion. We formulate reward adaptation as sampling from a reward-tilted target distribution and derive the corresponding Doob hh-transform of the masked discrete diffusion reverse kernel. The resulting guidance reweights categorical token-reveal transitions, in contrast to the additive drift or score correction used in continuous diffusion. The exact reference transform is kept separate from the executable approximations built on it.

  • •

    Executable finite-candidate sampler. We make the exact transform practical with a prediction-head hh-estimator, finite-candidate Doob-weighted selection, and an optional best-of-KK refinement for irreversible reveal decisions. The method uses only reward values and does not update the diffusion backbone. We characterize how tempering, sharpening, and terminal selection deviate from the exact target.

  • •

    Biological validation and trade-offs. We test the same frozen-backbone sampler on HepG2 enhancer design, cell-type-specific enhancer design, and protein inverse folding. D-DOIT improves over training-free baselines across the reported reward-guided design tasks, while preserving the relevant trade-offs in naturalness, motif structure, and inference budget.

Organization.

Section 2 reviews the masked discrete diffusion backbone, defines the reward-tilted target, and states the exact discrete Doob hh-transform. Section 3 develops the practical D-DOIT sampler, including the prediction-head hh-estimator, finite-candidate weighted update, and optional best-of-KK refinement. Section 4 reports experiments on regulatory DNA design, cell-type-specific enhancer design, and protein inverse folding. The appendix provides related work (Appendix A), the proof of the discrete Doob hh-transform (Appendix B), the standard masked diffusion sampler (Appendix E), and full experimental details (Appendices J, K and M).

2 Preliminaries

We first define the frozen masked diffusion reverse chain that serves as the base law for D-DOIT. We then state the reward-tilted target distribution and the discrete Doob hh-transform that transports this base law to the target without changing the model parameters [22, 23]. We keep the exact reference transform separate from the executable approximation built on it, which Section 3 develops.

2.1 Masked Discrete Diffusion Models

We specialize to masked discrete diffusion. Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be the clean token alphabet, d=|𝒱|d=|\mathcal{V}|, and 𝗆\mathsf{m} a special mask token. Define 𝒱~:=𝒱∪{𝗆}\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}:=\mathcal{V}\cup\{\mathsf{m}\}, with sequence spaces 𝒳=𝒱N\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{V}^{N} and 𝒳~=𝒱~N\widetilde{\mathcal{X}}=\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}^{N}. The data distribution is supported on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, while the forward process evolves on 𝒳~\widetilde{\mathcal{X}} by progressively replacing clean tokens with 𝗆\mathsf{m}. On the grid tl=l​T/Lt_{l}=lT/L, let bl∈[0,1]b_{l}\in[0,1] be the masking probability on [tl−1,tl][t_{l-1},t_{l}]. The single-token forward kernel is

qtl−1,tl(y∣x)=(1−bl)𝟏{y=x}+bl𝟏{y=𝗆},x,y∈𝒱~,\displaystyle q_{t_{l-1},t_{l}}(y\mid x)=(1-b_{l})\mathbf{1}\{y=x\}+b_{l}\mathbf{1}\{y=\mathsf{m}\},\quad x,y\in\widetilde{\mathcal{V}},

so with probability 1−bl1-b_{l} the token stays fixed and otherwise it jumps to the mask state; once masked it stays masked. With αl=∏r=1l(1−br)\alpha_{l}=\prod_{r=1}^{l}(1-b_{r}), a clean token x0∈𝒱x_{0}\in\mathcal{V} satisfies

q0,tl(y∣x0)=ℙ(Xtl=y∣X0=x0)=αl𝟏{y=x0}+(1−αl)𝟏{y=𝗆}.\displaystyle q_{0,t_{l}}(y\mid x_{0})=\mathbb{P}(X_{t_{l}}=y\mid X_{0}=x_{0})=\alpha_{l}\mathbf{1}\{y=x_{0}\}+(1-\alpha_{l})\mathbf{1}\{y=\mathsf{m}\}.

We choose αL≈0\alpha_{L}\approx 0 for a sufficiently large TT, so that q0,Tq_{0,T} is concentrated near the mask state. The forward masking process is applied independently across coordinates. The conditional one-step time reversal also has a closed form, and Appendix F records the forward transition matrices and the analytic reverse kernel that the learned sampler approximates.

Since 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} is unknown during generation, masked diffusion models approximate the clean-token posterior with a trained neural network. For each coordinate jj, let μθj(⋅∣𝐱tl,tl)∈Δ(𝒱)\mu_{\theta}^{j}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{t_{l}},t_{l})\in\Delta(\mathcal{V}) denote the neural network’s approximation to ℙ(X0j=⋅∣𝐗tl=𝐱tl)\mathbb{P}(X_{0}^{j}=\cdot\mid\mathbf{X}_{t_{l}}=\mathbf{x}_{t_{l}}). Plugging this approximation into the analytic reverse posterior gives the learned one-step reverse transition from tlt_{l} to tl−1t_{l-1}:

Finally, the learned reverse model factorizes over coordinates,

Pθ,tl​(𝐱tl−1∣𝐱tl)\displaystyle P_{\theta,t_{l}}(\mathbf{x}_{t_{l-1}}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t_{l}}) =∏j=1NPθ,tl​(xtl−1j∣𝐱tl).\displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{N}P_{\theta,t_{l}}(x_{t_{l-1}}^{j}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t_{l}}).

Starting from an initial masked state 𝐗¯tL\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{L}}, we iteratively sample 𝐗¯tl−1∼Pθ,tl(⋅∣𝐗¯tl)\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{l-1}}\sim P_{\theta,t_{l}}(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{l}}) from l=Ll=L to l=1l=1 and obtain the final clean sample 𝐗¯0\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{0}. We next define the target these modified transitions should realize.

2.2 Reward-tilted Target and Doob’s hh-transform

We now formalize the inference-time adaptation objective. Given a reward function R:𝒳→ℝR:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} and a temperature parameter β>0\beta>0, define the positive reward weight

ϕ⁡(𝐱0)=exp⁡(R⁡(𝐱0)/β).\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x}_{0})=\exp(R(\bx_0)/\beta). (2.2)

The desired clean-time target is the reward-tilted version of the frozen model law,

πβ​(𝐱0)\displaystyle\pi_{\beta}(\mathbf{x}_{0}) =pθ​(𝐱0)​ϕ​(𝐱0)Zβ,Zβ=𝔼𝐗0∼pθ​[ϕ⁡(𝐗0)].\displaystyle=\frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0})\phi(\mathbf{x}_{0})}{Z_{\beta}},\quad Z_{\beta}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}_{0}\sim p_{\theta}}\left[\phi(\mathbf{X}_{0})\right]. (2.3)

Thus adaptation is a distributional problem: change the terminal law from pθp_{\theta} to πβ\pi_{\beta} while preserving the frozen reverse chain as the base proposal. The discrete Doob hh-function is the object that makes this transport local in time and gives a kernel-level correction.

Definition 2.1 (Discrete Doob hh-function).

For the frozen reverse chain defined above, the discrete Doob hh-function is the downstream reward weight conditioned on a partially denoised state:

h(𝐱¯tl,tl)=𝔼pθ[exp⁡(R⁡(𝐗0)/β)∣𝐗¯tl=𝐱¯tl],l=0,…,L.\displaystyle h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}},t_{l})=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}}\left[\exp(R(\bX_0)/\beta)\mid\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{l}}=\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}}\right],\qquad l=0,\ldots,L. (2.4)

At clean time, this reduces to h⁡(𝐱0,0)=ϕ⁡(𝐱0)h(\mathbf{x}_{0},0)=\phi(\mathbf{x}_{0}). At an intermediate time, h⁡(𝐱¯tl,tl)h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}},t_{l}) is the reward-to-go under the frozen reverse chain. It therefore measures how promising the current partial sequence is for the terminal reward objective at clean time under the frozen process.

The next theorem states the exact kernel transform induced by this value function. It is the discrete analogue of the continuous Doob correction, but it acts by reweighting transition probabilities rather than by adding a vector field to a continuous score.

Theorem 2.1 (Discrete Doob’s hh-transform).

In the fully masked terminal setting, 𝐗¯tL\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{L}} is deterministic, so h⁡(𝐗¯tL,tL)=Zβh(\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{L}},t_{L})=Z_{\beta} and the terminal distribution is unchanged. Let hh be defined as in Definition 2.1. Then Doob’s hh-transform induces the reverse kernel

Pθ,tlh(𝐱¯tl−1∣𝐱¯tl)=Pθ,tl(𝐱¯tl−1∣𝐱¯tl)h⁡(𝐱¯tl−1,tl−1)h⁡(𝐱¯tl,tl),l=1,…,L.\displaystyle P_{\theta,t_{l}}^{h}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l-1}}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}})=P_{\theta,t_{l}}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l-1}}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}})\frac{h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1})}{h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}},t_{l})},\qquad l=1,\ldots,L. (2.5)

The resulting Doob-transformed reverse chain has marginal distribution

pθ,tlh(𝐱¯tl)=pθ,tl​(𝐱¯tl)​h​(𝐱¯tl,tl)Zβ,l=0,…,L,\displaystyle p_{\theta,t_{l}}^{h}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}})=\frac{p_{\theta,t_{l}}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}})h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}},t_{l})}{Z_{\beta}},\qquad l=0,\ldots,L,

In particular, since

h⁡(𝐱0,0)=exp⁡(R⁡(𝐱0)/β),\displaystyle h(\mathbf{x}_{0},0)=\exp(R(\bx_0)/\beta),

the clean-time marginal of the Doob-transformed reverse chain is exactly the reward-tilted distribution

pθ,0h​(𝐱¯0)=πβ​(𝐱¯0)=pθ,0​(𝐱¯0)​exp⁡(R⁡(𝐱¯0)/β)Zβ.\displaystyle p_{\theta,0}^{h}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{0})=\pi_{\beta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{0})=\frac{p_{\theta,0}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{0})\exp(R(\bar\bx_0)/\beta)}{Z_{\beta}}.

The proof is deferred to Appendix B. The theorem identifies the exact population object that D-DOIT approximates. If the downstream value ratio h⁡(𝐱¯tl−1,tl−1)/h⁡(𝐱¯tl,tl)h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1})/h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}},t_{l}) were available at every reverse step, then local reweighting of the frozen transition kernel would sample exactly from πβ\pi_{\beta} at clean time. This guarantee is a statement about the true rollout value and the exact normalized kernel, not the prediction-head implementation. In Section 3, the head proxy, finite candidate set, proposal and completion temperatures, weight sharpening, and terminal selection each have a distinct role. Finite-candidate convergence alone cannot remove a systematic value or proposal mismatch. We keep the original PP-referenced πβ\pi_{\beta} as the theoretical benchmark; Appendix B separately states the exact transform for a temperature-modified reference chain. The practical method in Section 3 estimates this ratio without retraining the masked diffusion model. The continuous analogue appears as an additive score correction ∇log⁡pt+∇log⁡ht\nabla\log p_{t}+\nabla\log h_{t}. The categorical and irreversible reverse dynamics of masked diffusion have no Euclidean score field, and instead require the multiplicative kernel reweighting in (2.5); Appendix C records the continuous derivation.

3 D-DOIT: A Discrete Sampler Based on Doob’s hh-transform

In this section, we introduce D-DOIT, a training-free sampler that guides a frozen masked discrete diffusion model toward the reward-tilted target in (2.3) using black-box rewards R:𝒳→ℝR:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} defined on clean sequences. The exact transform in Theorem 2.1 says what the sampler should do: reweight each frozen reverse kernel by the downstream value ratio of the discrete Doob hh-function. The challenge is computational, since evaluating this value exactly would require future denoising rollouts from every candidate next state. D-DOIT therefore follows an exact-object-to-estimator design: it estimates the downstream value with the frozen prediction head, approximates the transformed kernel with finite candidates, and optionally branches late to hedge irreversible token reveals. Figure 1 summarizes the construction.

3.1 D-DOIT Algorithm

The transformed kernel in (2.5) depends on the downstream value h⁡(𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)h(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1}) for each candidate reverse state 𝐲¯tl−1∈𝒳~\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{X}} reachable from the current state 𝐱¯tl\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}}. This subsection turns that exact identity into an executable sampler. The first component estimates each candidate’s downstream value with a prediction-head completion. The second component uses these values to form a finite-candidate approximation to the transformed kernel. The final component adds an optional best-of-KK refinement for the irreversible reveal structure of masked diffusion.

Prediction-head hh-estimator.

The exact value h⁡(𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)h(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1}) averages the reward weight over all complete denoising continuations from the candidate next state 𝐲¯tl−1\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}. Naive Monte Carlo would roll out the frozen reverse chain many times from every candidate. D-DOIT avoids these nested rollouts by evaluating candidates with the masked discrete diffusion prediction head at 𝐲¯tl−1\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}. Recall from Section 2.1 that μθj(⋅∣𝐱tl,tl)∈Δ(𝒱)\mu_{\theta}^{j}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{t_{l}},t_{l})\in\Delta(\mathcal{V}) denotes the neural network’s approximation to the clean-token posterior at coordinate jj. The head provides a direct clean-sequence completion distribution by fixing revealed tokens and independently sampling still-masked positions from the coordinate-wise clean-token posteriors μθj(⋅∣𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)\mu_{\theta}^{j}(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1}); we write pθheadp^{\mathrm{head}}_{\theta} for this direct completion law, which is not generally a rollout conditional:

pθhead(𝐱0∣𝐲¯tl−1)=∏j:y¯tl−1j≠𝗆δy¯tl−1j(x0j)∏j:y¯tl−1j=𝗆μθj(x0j∣𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1).\displaystyle p^{\mathrm{head}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}})=\prod_{\mathclap{j:\,\bar{y}_{t_{l-1}}^{j}\neq\mathsf{m}}}\delta_{\bar{y}_{t_{l-1}}^{j}}(x_{0}^{j})\prod_{\mathclap{j:\,\bar{y}_{t_{l-1}}^{j}=\mathsf{m}}}\mu_{\theta}^{j}(x_{0}^{j}\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1}). (3.1)
Definition 3.1 (Prediction-head hh-estimator).

For every reachable candidate reverse state 𝐲¯tl−1∈𝒳~\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{X}}, D-DOIT estimates the downstream value by the one-step clean-completion expectation under the factorized prediction-head distribution for each candidate state:

h¯θ​(𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)\displaystyle\bar{h}_{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1}) =𝔼𝐱0∼pθhead​(𝐱0∣𝐲¯tl−1)​[ϕ⁡(𝐱0)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim p^{\mathrm{head}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}})}\!\left[\phi(\mathbf{x}_{0})\right]. (3.2)

The estimator (3.2) replaces the rollout value h⁡(𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)h(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1}) from Definition 2.1 with a single-step completion value. This is the main approximation that makes the transform practical; Appendix D discusses its bias relative to full future rollouts. For each candidate, we estimate (3.2) with one tempered completion 𝐱^0∼pθ,γhead(⋅∣𝐲¯tl−1)\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\sim p^{\mathrm{head}}_{\theta,\gamma}(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}):

h^​(𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)\displaystyle\hat{h}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1}) =exp⁡(R⁡(𝐱^0)/β),𝐱^0∼pθ,γhead(⋅∣𝐲¯tl−1),\displaystyle=\exp(R(\hat\bx_0)/\beta),\qquad\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\sim p^{\mathrm{head}}_{\theta,\gamma}(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}), (3.3)
μθ,γj​(v∣𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)\displaystyle\mu_{\theta,\gamma}^{j}(v\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1}) ∝μθj​(v∣𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)1/γ.\displaystyle\propto\mu_{\theta}^{j}(v\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1})^{1/\gamma}. (3.4)

The completion temperature γ\gamma tempers the completion of a candidate 𝐲¯tl−1\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}} into a clean sequence. Smaller γ\gamma sharpens the completion toward the model mode, while larger γ\gamma smooths noisy predictions. Because the reward is queried only on the sampled prediction-head completion 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}, R⁡(⋅)R(\cdot) need not be differentiable, and no gradients are backpropagated through the reward oracle. Using nhn_{h} independent completions per candidate averages

h^nh​(𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)\displaystyle\hat{h}_{n_{h}}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1}) =1nh∑i=1nhexp⁡(R⁡(𝐱^0(i))/β),𝐱^0(i)∼pθ,γhead(⋅∣𝐲¯tl−1),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{h}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{h}}\exp(R(\hat\bx_0^{(i)})/\beta),\qquad\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{(i)}\sim p^{\mathrm{head}}_{\theta,\gamma}(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}), (3.5)

which reduces Monte Carlo variance for this head expectation without removing its discrepancy from the rollout value. The reported main configurations use nh=1n_{h}=1.

Finite-candidate discrete hh-transform.

At reverse step ll, D-DOIT first draws MM candidate next states {𝐲¯tl−1(m)}m=1M\{\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}^{(m)}\}_{m=1}^{M} from a τ\tau-tempered masked discrete diffusion proposal:

μθ,τj​(v∣𝐱¯tl,tl)∝μθj​(v∣𝐱¯tl,tl)1/τ,v∈𝒱.\displaystyle\mu_{\theta,\tau}^{j}(v\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}},t_{l})\propto\mu_{\theta}^{j}(v\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}},t_{l})^{1/\tau},\qquad v\in\mathcal{V}. (3.6)

Both temperatures act on the same coordinate-wise prediction head μθj\mu_{\theta}^{j}, but they play different roles: τ\tau controls proposal diversity, while γ\gamma controls the clean completion used for reward scoring. We draw each candidate 𝐲¯tl−1(m)\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}^{(m)} from the masked discrete diffusion reverse kernel (2.1) with pθ,τp_{\theta,\tau} in place of pθp_{\theta}, keeping the schedule factor (αl−1−αl)/(1−αl)(\alpha_{l-1}-\alpha_{l})/(1-\alpha_{l}) and the copy-through rule. All MM proposals share one forward pass, and each is completed once via (3.3). The next state 𝐱¯tl−1=𝐲¯tl−1(m∗)\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l-1}}=\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}^{(m^{*})} is drawn by sampling the index m∗m^{*} over the MM candidates, each assigned probability

w(m)=h^​(𝐲¯tl−1(m),tl−1)ω∑r=1Mh^​(𝐲¯tl−1(r),tl−1)ω.\displaystyle w^{(m)}=\frac{\hat{h}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}^{(m)},t_{l-1})^{\omega}}{\sum_{r=1}^{M}\hat{h}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}^{(r)},t_{l-1})^{\omega}}. (3.7)

With τ=1\tau=1, (3.7) is a finite-candidate self-normalized approximation to the hh-reweighted transition induced by (2.5), with ω\omega controlling how sharply the sampler follows the estimated downstream value. For one completion, h^ω=exp⁡(ω​R​(𝐱^0)/β)\hat{h}^{\omega}=\exp(\omega R(\hat\bx_0)/\beta), so ω\omega is not a separate approximation. Every (ω,β)(\omega,\beta) pair is equivalent to ω=1\omega=1 with effective inverse temperature η=ω/β\eta=\omega/\beta, the parameter used in Appendix B. With τ>1\tau>1, the proposal is deliberately smoothed, so the weighted selection rule becomes a biased proposal approximation that we use to maintain candidate diversity. Retaining the original PP-referenced target under a smoothed proposal would instead require the importance weight

w~(m)∝Pθ,tl​(𝐲¯tl−1(m)∣𝐱¯tl)Qlτ​(𝐲¯tl−1(m)∣𝐱¯tl)​h​(𝐲¯tl−1(m),tl−1),\displaystyle\widetilde{w}^{(m)}\propto\frac{P_{\theta,t_{l}}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}^{(m)}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}})}{Q^{\tau}_{l}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}^{(m)}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}})}h(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}^{(m)},t_{l-1}), (3.8)

where QlτQ^{\tau}_{l} is the proposal kernel, assuming its support covers the target transition. Our operating points omit this ratio, so it is a reference correction, not the executed algorithm. Even with it, a biased proxy, sharpening, and terminal best-of-KK selection would remain. A guided step costs 1+M1+M model-side NFE: one shared proposal pass and MM completion passes. It also costs MM reward evaluations; Appendix G gives the full accounting and cost conventions.

Best-of-KK refinement.

Revealed tokens cannot be revised, so D-DOIT optionally duplicates each active trajectory into KK copies after split update ssplits_{\mathrm{split}}, counted in reverse updates. The copies continue independently, and the method keeps the highest-reward clean sequence within each group. For each original trajectory bb, the selected output is

𝐱0(b)=𝐱0(b,kb∗),kb∗=argmaxk∈{1,…,K}R⁡(𝐱0(b,k)).\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{0}^{(b)}=\mathbf{x}_{0}^{(b,k_{b}^{*})},\qquad k_{b}^{*}=\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}R(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{(b,k)}). (3.9)

The K×K\times multiplier is paid only after the split, hedging early decisions without always multiplying the full trajectory cost. This terminal argmax changes the output law and cannot repair earlier reveals. Before the split a trajectory is shared; after it the KK copies update independently, and with K=1K=1 or ssplit=Ls_{\mathrm{split}}=L the method reduces to D-DOIT. Appendices H and H in the appendix give the sampler and its per-step guided update.

3.2 Two Configurations: D-DOIT-LBOK-S and D-DOIT-Q

We report two operating points of the same sampler that differ only in budget allocation. D-DOIT-LBOK-S uses a small per-step candidate budget plus late best-of-KK refinement for the practical lower-budget regime. D-DOIT-Q allocates more inference budget to candidate evaluation and/or split-time refinement to test the quality frontier of the frozen backbone. Table 5 lists the benchmark-specific values, and Section 4 evaluates both configurations against training-free and training-based baselines.

4 Experiments

In this section, we include the following results: (1) regulatory DNA enhancer design (Section 4.1); (2) cell-type-specific enhancer design (Section 4.2); (3) protein inverse folding (Section 4.3); (4) contrast with the closest reward-guided sampling baselines (Section 4.4); (5) analysis of the estimation accuracy of 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} (Section 4.5); (6) analysis of the impact of different reward functions (Section 4.6).

Furthermore, we conducted detailed ablation studies on the D-DOIT algorithm using the regulatory DNA sequence design task to analyze the relationship between its computational efficiency and performance, and compared it with other algorithms (Appendices J and L). The task cell type specific enhancer design also features a detailed efficiency-performance analysis (Appendix K. Detailed experimental setups are also provided for the protein inverse folding task, serving as a complement to cross-modal transfer (Appendix M). Table 1 shows the differences between our algorithm and several other algorithms.

4.1 Task 1: Regulatory DNA Sequence Design

Regulatory DNA elements direct cell-type-specific gene expression. They form an important target for gene therapy [24]. We use the HepG2 enhancer design benchmark of [8]: generate 200200 bp enhancer sequences with high predicted HepG2 activity and natural enhancer statistics on a frozen masked discrete diffusion backbone. The dataset, reward oracle, checkpoint, protocol, metrics, and baselines are documented in Sections J.1 and J.2.

Table 2 reports quality metrics. D-DOIT-Q outperforms every training-free baseline in Table 2 on every metric. D-DOIT-Q reaches 6.196.19 Pred-Activity, 91.7%91.7\% ATAC-Acc, 0.8940.894 3-mer Corr, and 0.9230.923 JASPAR Corr. It exceeds training-based DRAKES on Pred-Activity, 3-mer Corr, and JASPAR Corr, while remaining slightly lower on ATAC-Acc (91.7%91.7\% vs. 92.5%92.5\%). The near-TDS-speed D-DOIT-LBOK-S matches TDS on Pred-Activity (4.564.56 vs. 4.584.58) while lifting ATAC-Acc from 40.0%40.0\% to 65.0%65.0\%, 3-mer Corr from 0.8170.817 to 0.8510.851, and JASPAR Corr from 0.7980.798 to 0.9480.948 over TDS. At a similar measured wall-clock budget, Q improves all four metric means over SVDD-PM and improves activity, accessibility, and 3-mer correlation over Frozen Best-of-732; endpoint search retains higher JASPAR correlation. Sections J.3 and 6 gives the matched-time results and full protocol. A guided step costs 1+M1+M model forward passes plus MM reward evaluations. The high-budget Q row is calibrated to endpoint sampling at approximately 10.610.6 seconds per output on the same A100; Appendix G gives the accounting.

4.2 Task 2: Cell-type-specific Enhancer Design

Cell-type-specific enhancer design asks for sequences active in a target cell line and silent in off-target cell lines. This task is a stricter test of controllable generation than Section 4.1. We conduct experiments on the Ctrl-DNA enhancer benchmark of [25]. The benchmark spans three cell lines (HepG2, K562, SK-N-SH) and supplies cell-type-specific Enformer-based reward oracles. The dataset, composite specificity reward, per-cell-line oracles, diffusion training details, and the baseline-tuning protocol are documented in Sections K.1 and K.3.

We report specificity (Δ​R\Delta R), Motif Corr, and set-level diversity; Δ​R\Delta R is the target-cell oracle score minus the average off-target score. Baselines include the training-free methods as in Section 4.1, regLM [26], RL baselines [25], and directed evolution; full metric definitions and baseline tuning are documented in the appendix, Sections K.2 and K.3.

Table 3 reports three-cell-line averages. Among the diffusion-guidance baselines, D-DOIT clearly improves specificity: D-DOIT-LBOK-S raises Δ​R\Delta R from 0.0020.002 to 0.0330.033 over TDS while improving Motif Corr from 0.5730.573 to 0.6480.648 at near-TDS wall-clock. D-DOIT-Q pushes Δ​R\Delta R to 0.1190.119 while trading motif preservation for reward, giving the high-specificity point; LBOK-S remains the lower-budget point. Under the matched-time control, endpoint search also improves specificity and captures much of this gain, unlike the larger activity and accessibility separation on DRAKES. Q’s mean differences from Frozen Best-of-708 are small and are not claimed statistically significant, so the specificity gain is not unique to D-DOIT here. Wall-clock, per-cell, and diversity details and the matched-time control are in Sections K.4 and K.5.

4.3 Task 3: Protein Inverse Folding

To test a different sequence space and reward, we apply D-DOIT to the DRAKES protein inverse-folding benchmark [8], using its reward oracle and evaluation metrics. Here the target backbone is fixed and the sampler generates amino-acid sequences. We evaluate predicted stability and agreement between the predicted structure and that backbone, with the full cross-method comparison including every reported metric for this benchmark in Table 3.

Across all 1212 test backbones, three seeds, and 128128 sequences per backbone and seed, D-DOIT achieves joint success of 68.1±3.5%68.1\pm 3.5\%, compared with the published SMC and TDS results of 63.6%63.6\% and 62.9%62.9\% (Table 3). The configuration M=52M=52, K=8K=8, nh=1n_{h}=1 was fixed before test evaluation, with no post-test tuning, and each entry reports the mean and sample SD across the three seed-level metrics. D-DOIT has the highest predicted stability and joint success among the six methods, while TDS has better structural fidelity. The other five rows are taken from DRAKES Table 2, not rerun or compute-matched controls. Appendix M gives the full protocol. This supports transfer to a second biological sequence-design task, not experimental protein validation.

4.4 Compute–quality Trade-off

To compare compute across methods, we account for oracle reward calls in addition to model evaluations. A guided update evaluates a shared proposal head, MM candidate heads, and one reward per completed candidate; branching adds work only after the split.

The lower-budget DRAKES setting uses 1,9701{,}970 model evaluations and 1,7731{,}773 candidate completions per output, with 1,7771{,}777 reward evaluations after ranking the four final branches. Terminal ranking adds up to KK queries when scores are not cached. In the 640640-output diagnostic, 1,2901{,}290 vectorized oracle calls score 1,137,2801{,}137{,}280 sequences, so physical calls and scored sequences are distinct cost units. Full accounting is given in Appendix G.

Model NFE alone therefore does not determine total compute. In Table 7, Frozen Best-of-15 has a similar model budget (1,9201{,}920 versus 1,9701{,}970 evaluations per output) but only 1515 rather than 1,7771{,}777 oracle evaluations. Its 640640-output job is faster (97.897.8 versus 327.8327.8 seconds) but has lower Pred-Activity (2.2192.219 versus 4.4914.491). Thus, this comparison approximately matches model budget, not wall-clock time. The calibration in Table 6 instead matches endpoint sampling to Q at approximately 10.610.6 seconds per output.

LBOK-S remains the near-TDS-runtime operating point (1.16×1.16\times in the main timing study), whereas Q allocates substantially more compute to quality. For Ctrl-DNA, Q and Frozen Best-of-708 take 5.435.43 and 5.515.51 seconds per output on the same A100. Because absolute timings depend on batching and memory use, we report each study under its own timing protocol. D-DOIT generation costs recur for new samples, and comparisons with training-based methods concern sample quality rather than matched or amortized training cost.

4.5 Completion Quality and Search Diagnostics

A crucial aspect of estimating hh is how to obtain 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}; while a common approach to maintaining speed is to estimate 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} directly from xtx_{t} in a single step, a more refined method involves obtaining 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} through iterative steps starting from xtx_{t}. To better compare these two approaches, we investigated the performance of different estimation methods. Increasing completions per candidate from nh=1n_{h}=1 to 22 and 33 raises final guidance reward RR from 5.272±0.0575.272\pm 0.057 to 5.764±0.0335.764\pm 0.033 and 5.978±0.0265.978\pm 0.026, at 41%41\% and 81%81\% additional wall time; we retain nh=1n_{h}=1 as the default. Direct and sequential completions have similar hh-value distributions (Wasserstein-1 0.0600.060–0.1240.124; Section L.5), supporting practical use without exact-target equivalence.

4.6 Oracle Robustness

The choice of reward function is independent of the D-DOIT algorithm itself, yet it significantly influences the algorithm’s performance. A more accurate reward function provides better guidance for the D-DOIT algorithm. To examine this, we designed various reward functions and observed their guiding effects. Replacing RR with Enformer, CNN, or MLP predictions improves all four metrics over unguided sampling (Table 8); Pred-Activity reaches 4.4914.491, 2.2032.203, and 1.5441.544, versus 0.3710.371 for the frozen model. Held-out rescoring preserves these gains (Table 9), while evaluator scales remain incomparable. The controls support robustness across tested predictors without establishing experimental biological activity and are distinct from the high-budget 6.19±0.056.19\pm 0.05 result.

5 Conclusion and Discussion

We introduced D-DOIT, a training-free sampler that applies Doob’s hh-transform directly to frozen masked discrete diffusion models. Using a prediction-head hh-estimator and finite-candidate Doob-weighted selection, D-DOIT supports black-box rewards without reward gradients or backbone retraining. Across DRAKES HepG2, Ctrl-DNA, and protein inverse folding, D-DOIT outperforms training-free guidance baselines, although its highest-quality results require a larger compute budget.

The method has three main limitations. First, practical approximations, including temperature scaling, sharpening, and best-of-KK selection, may introduce bias and do not retain the exact-target guarantee; late branching also cannot revise revealed tokens. Second, evaluation relies on predictive biological benchmarks and requires experimental validation. Third, the highest-quality setting incurs substantial recurring inference cost, leaving the reward–compute trade-off as a practical challenge. Overall, Doob-style kernel reweighting provides a general framework for guiding discrete generative models with sequence-level rewards.

Appendix

Appendix A Related Work

We review related work on reward-guided adaptation of discrete diffusion and flow models, as well as regulatory DNA sequence design.

Reward-guided adaptation of discrete diffusion and flow models.

Reward-guided generation has proved effective for aligning language models [27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32] and diffusion models [33, 34, 35] with task-specific objectives. In discrete generative models, however, guidance must act on categorical transitions over a finite vocabulary. Early discrete denoising diffusion models use structured categorical or absorbing-state corruption [1, 36, 2]; masked discrete diffusion models scale a simple absorbing-mask objective [3, 4]; score-entropy and ratio-matching parameterizations form a non-masked alternative [5, 37]; and discrete flow matching extends the same idea to a flow framework [38, 39]. Reward adaptation for these models can be training-based or training-free. Training-based methods include DRAKES, which finetunes the generator through reward backpropagation [8], trajectory-level alignment [9], and reinforcement learning (RL)-style finetuning methods developed for continuous diffusion [40, 41, 42, 43]; these methods change backbone weights and need a differentiable reward. Training-free methods instead steer a frozen backbone at inference time, including Sequential Monte Carlo and twisted sampling [11, 44, 45], posterior sampling for inverse problems [46], soft value-based decoding [12], reward-guided iterative refinement [13], clean-sample Markov chains [47], simple guidance for masked discrete diffusion [14], denoising posterior prediction [15], plug-and-play control [16], and inference-time scaling [17, 48]. These methods steer a frozen backbone, but they do not directly tilt the discrete reverse kernel toward an optimal proposal.

Comparing with three representative efforts highlights the distinct role of D-DOIT. DRAKES [8] provides a strong reward-optimization baseline, but it finetunes the backbone and requires a differentiable reward. Soft value-based decoding [12] selects candidates using importance scores on intermediate latents, but it does not tilt the reverse transition kernel itself. Simple masked-diffusion guidance [14] introduces a heuristic guidance term, but lacks an explicit optimality target. In contrast, D-DOIT is the first inference-time method to implement an executable estimator of Doob’s hh-transform for the discrete reverse kernel [49, 19, 20, 21, 50]. It scores candidates through the resulting hh-tilted kernel, combines a frozen masked discrete diffusion backbone with a black-box reward, and further supports optional best-of-KK refinement over the same frozen prior. Because finite-candidate value-weighted selection also appears in soft value-based decoding and related methods, we do not claim that local candidate selection is unique to D-DOIT. CDM [51] learns a twist to amortize value estimation, and DPRM [52] applies Doob-derived corrections to token ordering while retaining a host token sampler; CSMC [47] instead searches over clean samples. Our distinction is the explicit categorical reverse-kernel hh-transform as the reference object, evaluated with a frozen prediction-head proxy rather than a learned value network.

Regulatory DNA sequence design.

Regulatory DNA design aims to generate sequences that score well under predictive assays and stay faithful to natural regulatory grammar. Oracle-guided optimization with experimental validation drives early machine-guided enhancer design [53, 24, 54]; autoregressive regulatory language models [26] and genomic foundation models [55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60] provide strong sequence priors; and diffusion-based generators specialize these priors through Dirichlet diffusion and score-entropy variants [6, 7, 61]. For reward-optimization benchmarks, DRAKES evaluates HepG2 enhancer generation through activity, accessibility, kk-mer, and motif-structure metrics [8]; Ctrl-DNA studies cell-type-specific enhancer design through constrained reinforcement learning [25]; and concurrent work combines discrete diffusion with tree search for cell-type-specific regulatory DNA design under related biological reward objectives [62]. The strongest methods on these benchmarks share one limit: they reach high reward only through backbone updates, policy training, or expanded inference search.

Comparing with three representative efforts highlights the efficiency and generality of D-DOIT. DRAKES [8] finetunes the backbone and requires a differentiable reward. Ctrl-DNA [25] achieves cell-type specificity through constrained RL with reward signals shaped for policy optimization. The concurrent tree-search method of Awasthi et al. [62] remains training-free at inference time, but expands a search tree over partial sequences and increases the per-step sampling cost. In contrast, D-DOIT is the first method to compete on both benchmarks without policy training. It trades modest inference-time compute for reward gains while preserving near-base per-step cost.

hτ,η​(𝐱¯,tl)\displaystyle h_{\tau,\eta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}},t_{l}) =𝔼ℚτ​[exp⁡(η​R​(𝐗0))∣𝐗¯tl=𝐱¯].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}^{\tau}}[\exp(\eta R(\bX_0))\mid\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{l}}=\bar{\mathbf{x}}].

Then the kernels

Qlτ,h​(𝐲¯∣𝐱¯)\displaystyle Q^{\tau,h}_{l}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}}) =Qlτ​(𝐲¯∣𝐱¯)​hτ,η​(𝐲¯,tl−1)hτ,η​(𝐱¯,tl)\displaystyle=Q^{\tau}_{l}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}})\frac{h_{\tau,\eta}(\bar{\mathbf{y}},t_{l-1})}{h_{\tau,\eta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}},t_{l})}

are normalized. Starting from the same deterministic mask, their clean-time marginal is

q0τ,h​(𝐱0)\displaystyle q^{\tau,h}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{0}) =q0τ​(𝐱0)​exp⁡(η​R​(𝐱0))Zτ,η.\displaystyle=\frac{q^{\tau}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{0})\exp(\eta R(\bx_0))}{Z_{\tau,\eta}}.
Proof.

The Markov and tower properties give

hτ,η​(𝐱¯,tl)\displaystyle h_{\tau,\eta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}},t_{l}) =∑𝐲¯Qlτ​(𝐲¯∣𝐱¯)​hτ,η​(𝐲¯,tl−1),\displaystyle=\sum_{\bar{\mathbf{y}}}Q^{\tau}_{l}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}})h_{\tau,\eta}(\bar{\mathbf{y}},t_{l-1}),

which proves normalization and positivity on the reference support. At clean time hτ,η​(𝐱0,0)=exp⁡(η​R​(𝐱0))h_{\tau,\eta}(\mathbf{x}_{0},0)=\exp(\eta R(\bx_0)); at the deterministic initial mask hτ,η​(𝗆N,tL)=Zτ,ηh_{\tau,\eta}(\mathsf{m}^{N},t_{L})=Z_{\tau,\eta}. Consequently, the likelihood ratio of the transformed path law to ℚτ\mathbb{Q}^{\tau} telescopes to

∏l=1Lhτ,η​(𝐱¯tl−1,tl−1)hτ,η​(𝐱¯tl,tl)\displaystyle\prod_{l=1}^{L}\frac{h_{\tau,\eta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1})}{h_{\tau,\eta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}},t_{l})} =exp⁡(η​R​(𝐱0))Zτ,η.\displaystyle=\frac{\exp(\eta R(\bx_0))}{Z_{\tau,\eta}}.

Marginalizing this identity over the intermediate states yields the claimed clean-time law. ∎

For τ=1\tau=1, η=1/β\eta=1/\beta this recovers the PP-reference theorem. Otherwise the target changes; the practical proxy, windowing, and terminal selection do not inherit its exactness.

Appendix C Continuous-time Doob’s hh-transform on Score-based Diffusion

We record the standard continuous-time derivation for comparison with the discrete construction. Consider a forward score-based diffusion on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d},

d𝐗t=f⁡(𝐗t,t)​dt+g⁡(t)​d𝐖t,t∈[0,T],\displaystyle\differential\mathbf{X}_{t}=f(\mathbf{X}_{t},t)\,\differential t+g(t)\,\differential\mathbf{W}_{t},\qquad t\in[0,T],

with marginal density ptp_{t} and 𝐗0∼p0\mathbf{X}_{0}\sim p_{0}. The reverse-time process admits the well-known form

d𝐗t=(f(𝐗t,t)−g(t)2∇logpt(𝐗t))dt+g(t)d𝐖¯t,\displaystyle\differential\mathbf{X}_{t}=\bigl(f(\mathbf{X}_{t},t)-g(t)^{2}\nabla\log p_{t}(\mathbf{X}_{t})\bigr)\,\differential t+g(t)\,\differential\overline{\mathbf{W}}_{t},

where 𝐖¯t\overline{\mathbf{W}}_{t} is reverse-time Brownian motion [63]. For the continuous analogue of the reward-tilted target in (2.3), write the base terminal density as p0p_{0} and denote the target by π⁡(𝐱0)∝p0​(𝐱0)​ϕ​(𝐱0)\pi(\mathbf{x}_{0})\propto p_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{0})\phi(\mathbf{x}_{0}). Define the hh-function

ht​(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[ϕ⁡(𝐗0)|𝐗t=𝐱].\displaystyle h_{t}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}\big[\phi(\mathbf{X}_{0})\,\big|\,\mathbf{X}_{t}=\mathbf{x}\big].

Doob’s hh-transform replaces ptp_{t} with the tilted marginal p~t∝pt​ht\tilde{p}_{t}\propto p_{t}h_{t}, which gives the tilted reverse drift

(f(𝐱,t)−g(t)2∇logpt(𝐱))−g(t)2∇loght(𝐱)=f(𝐱,t)−g(t)2∇log(pt(𝐱)ht(𝐱)).\displaystyle\bigl(f(\mathbf{x},t)-g(t)^{2}\nabla\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)-g(t)^{2}\nabla\log h_{t}(\mathbf{x})=f(\mathbf{x},t)-g(t)^{2}\nabla\log\bigl(p_{t}(\mathbf{x})h_{t}(\mathbf{x})\bigr).

Equivalently, the score is shifted by an additive correction:

∇log⁡pt​(𝐱)⟶∇log⁡pt​(𝐱)+∇log⁡ht​(𝐱).\displaystyle\nabla\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x})\;\longrightarrow\;\nabla\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x})+\nabla\log h_{t}(\mathbf{x}).

With initialization from the tilted marginal at time TT, the terminal law of the tilted reverse process is π\pi [19, 20, 21]; using the base marginal at TT is exact only when that marginal is unchanged by the tilt. The continuous construction requires sufficient regularity of hth_{t} for ∇log⁡ht\nabla\log h_{t} to exist, not differentiability of RR itself. Under suitable smoothing and integrability conditions, differentiating a transition density can give this correction even for a black-box reward. The structural distinction for masked discrete diffusion is instead that 𝒳~\widetilde{\mathcal{X}} is categorical and has no Euclidean score field. Section 3 therefore formulates a discrete kernel-level analogue, where the tilt enters as a multiplicative reweighting of categorical transition probabilities.

Appendix D On the Prediction-head hh-estimator

Definition 3.1 is the executable counterpart of the rollout h-function used by the exact discrete transform. For attention-based masked discrete diffusion models, it is generally an estimator rather than an exact identity. For a candidate state 𝐲¯tl−1\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}} at time tl−1t_{l-1}, the exact quantity is

h⁡(𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)=𝔼pθ​[ϕ⁡(𝐗0)∣𝐗¯tl−1=𝐲¯tl−1],\displaystyle h(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1})=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}}[\phi(\mathbf{X}_{0})\mid\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{l-1}}=\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}],

where the expectation runs over the pre-trained reverse chain from time tl−1t_{l-1} down to clean time, conditional on 𝐗¯tl−1=𝐲¯tl−1\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{l-1}}=\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}. At each subsequent reverse step l′∈{l−1,l−2,…,1}l^{\prime}\in\{l-1,l-2,\ldots,1\}, the reverse kernel (2.1) reveals each still-masked position from μθj​(x0j∣𝐱¯tl′,tl′)\mu_{\theta}^{j}(x_{0}^{j}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l^{\prime}}},t_{l^{\prime}}) and treats positions as conditionally independent. The copy flag freezes any position that the chain has already revealed. The exact rollout marginal of 𝐗0\mathbf{X}_{0} given 𝐗¯tl−1=𝐲¯tl−1\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{l-1}}=\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}} therefore mixes per-position predictions at the intermediate states 𝐱¯tl′\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l^{\prime}}} that the chain visits, which carry more revealed context than 𝐲¯tl−1\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}.

The factorized head (3.1) evaluates the clean completion from the current state 𝐲¯tl−1\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}} itself, giving

pθhead(𝐱0∣𝐲¯tl−1)=∏j:y¯tl−1j=𝗆μθj(x0j∣𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)⋅∏j:y¯tl−1j≠𝗆δy¯tl−1j(x0j).\displaystyle p^{\mathrm{head}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}})=\prod_{j:\,\bar{y}_{t_{l-1}}^{j}=\mathsf{m}}\mu_{\theta}^{j}(x_{0}^{j}\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1})\cdot\prod_{j:\,\bar{y}_{t_{l-1}}^{j}\neq\mathsf{m}}\delta_{\bar{y}_{t_{l-1}}^{j}}(x_{0}^{j}). (D.1)

A sufficient condition for this distribution to coincide with the full rollout marginal is that each still-masked coordinate’s head prediction remains invariant across all reachable subsequent contexts and times until that coordinate is revealed. For attention-based masked discrete diffusion models this invariance need not hold. The direct completion law therefore generally differs from the multi-step rollout law, even with arbitrarily many completion samples. To separate sampling noise from this distributional mismatch, let nhn_{h} denote the number of independent completions of a fixed candidate (reserving NN for sequence length), as in (3.5), and write

h^nh​(𝐲¯,t)\displaystyle\hat{h}_{n_{h}}(\bar{\mathbf{y}},t) =1nh∑i=1nhexp⁡(R⁡(𝐱^0(i))/β),𝐱^0(i)∼pθ,γhead(⋅∣𝐲¯),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{h}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{h}}\exp(R(\hat\bx_0^{(i)})/\beta),\qquad\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{(i)}\sim p^{\mathrm{head}}_{\theta,\gamma}(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}),
h¯θ,γ​(𝐲¯,t)\displaystyle\bar{h}_{\theta,\gamma}(\bar{\mathbf{y}},t) =𝔼pheadθ,γ(⋅∣𝐲¯)[exp⁡(R⁡(𝐗0)/β)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p^{\mathrm{head}}_{\theta,\gamma}(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}})}[\exp(R(\bX_0)/\beta)].

The executed single-completion estimator has nh=1n_{h}=1. As nh→∞n_{h}\to\infty, the sample average converges to h¯θ,γ\bar{h}_{\theta,\gamma}, not generally to the rollout value hh; at γ=1\gamma=1 it recovers the head expectation in (3.2).

Remark D.1 (Practical tempering and selection bias).

Completion temperature γ≠1\gamma\neq 1 changes the direct completion law and hence its reward expectation; it does not merely reduce Monte Carlo noise. Proposal temperature τ≠1\tau\neq 1 changes the candidate kernel, denoted QlτQ^{\tau}_{l}, relative to Pθ,tlP_{\theta,t_{l}}. With independent candidate draws and completion randomness, the large-MM limit of the uncorrected selection rule at a fixed current state 𝐱¯\bar{\mathbf{x}} is proportional to

Qlτ​(𝐲¯∣𝐱¯)​𝔼​[h^nh​(𝐲¯,tl−1)ω∣𝐲¯].\displaystyle Q^{\tau}_{l}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}})\,\mathbb{E}[\hat{h}_{n_{h}}(\bar{\mathbf{y}},t_{l-1})^{\omega}\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}].

On the proposal support, multiplying each weight by Pθ,tl​(𝐲¯∣𝐱¯)/Qlτ​(𝐲¯∣𝐱¯)P_{\theta,t_{l}}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}})/Q^{\tau}_{l}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}}) as in (3.8) corrects only this proposal mismatch, provided the proposal covers the base-kernel support. It does not correct the head-versus-rollout mismatch, completion tempering, nonlinear sharpening, or finite-MM self-normalization. The executed sampler omits this likelihood ratio; its uncorrected tempered update is not the exact PθP_{\theta} transform.

In particular, 𝔼⁡[h^nhω∣𝐲¯]\mathbb{E}[\hat{h}_{n_{h}}^{\omega}\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}] generally differs from (𝔼⁡[h^nh∣𝐲¯])ω(\mathbb{E}[\hat{h}_{n_{h}}\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}])^{\omega} and from h​(𝐲¯,t)ωh(\bar{\mathbf{y}},t)^{\omega}. Even with exact rollout values, raising 𝔼P​[exp⁡(R/β)∣𝐲¯]\mathbb{E}_{P}[\exp(R/\beta)\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}] to ω\omega is generally not the same as computing 𝔼P​[exp⁡(ω​R/β)∣𝐲¯]\mathbb{E}_{P}[\exp(\omega R/\beta)\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}]. For nh=1n_{h}=1, sharpening does yield an expectation of exp⁡(ω​R/β)\exp(\omega R/\beta) under the direct completion law, but that law is still not the rollout law. A separate exact transform relative to a tempered reference chain is stated in Appendix B; it requires that chain’s true downstream expectation, not the practical estimator. Finally, restricting guidance to a window omits exact transformed updates outside that window, and terminal best-of-KK ranking generally changes the output law even if each branch were sampled exactly. Thus these operating choices are not a guarantee of sampling (2.3); their empirical effects are studied in Section L.3.

Remark D.2 (Comparison with the continuous case).

The continuous-time h-function identity in [19] differentiates the Gaussian transition density to bypass the requirement that ϕ\phi be differentiable. The discrete construction avoids differentiating through ϕ\phi for a different reason: we query ϕ\phi only on a sampled clean completion 𝐱^0∼pθ,γhead(⋅∣𝐲¯tl−1)\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\sim p^{\mathrm{head}}_{\theta,\gamma}(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}), so a single forward pass through the prediction head suffices to produce h^​(𝐲¯tl−1,tl−1)=ϕ⁡(𝐱^0)\hat{h}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1})=\phi(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}) as in (3.3). The trade-off is that this single-shot estimator uses the factorized prediction head (3.1) instead of explicitly simulating the multi-step rollout marginal under the frozen reverse chain.

Appendix E Standard Masked Discrete Diffusion Sampling

Algorithm 1 records the standard generative process of the pre-trained masked discrete diffusion model [3] that D-DOIT builds on, provided here as background. The forward process corrupts tokens with an absorbing 𝗆\mathsf{m} state. The reverse process evaluates the clean-sequence prediction head pθhead​(𝐱0∣𝐱¯tl)p^{\mathrm{head}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}}) at each step. It then unmasks each still-masked position with the per-step reveal schedule from (2.1) and treats positions as conditionally independent. Once a step reveals a token, later steps freeze it. For consistency with the main text, Algorithm 1 writes a linear schedule with αtl=1−l/L\alpha_{t_{l}}=1-l/L; other monotone schedules can be substituted.

Appendix F Masked Diffusion Transition Details

This section records the explicit matrices behind the forward and reverse kernels summarized in Section 2.1. For x∈𝒱~x\in\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}, let ex∈ℝd+1e_{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1} be its one-hot vector including e𝗆e_{\mathsf{m}} for the mask token, and let 𝟏∈ℝd+1\mathbf{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1} be the all-one vector. Let (Xtl)l=0L(X_{t_{l}})_{l=0}^{L} be the single-token chain with X0∈𝒱X_{0}\in\mathcal{V}. Under the column-vector convention, the forward transition matrix on [tl−1,tl][t_{l-1},t_{l}] is

Kl=(1−bl)I+ble𝗆𝟏⊤,l=1,…,L,\displaystyle K_{l}=(1-b_{l})I+b_{l}e_{\mathsf{m}}\mathbf{1}^{\top},\quad l=1,\ldots,L,

so the transition matrix from time 00 to tlt_{l} is K¯l=KlKl−1⋯K1=αlI+(1−αl)e𝗆𝟏⊤,\bar{K}_{l}=K_{l}K_{l-1}\cdots K_{1}=\alpha_{l}I+(1-\alpha_{l})e_{\mathsf{m}}\mathbf{1}^{\top}, for αl=∏r=1l(1−br)\alpha_{l}=\prod_{r=1}^{l}(1-b_{r}). The conditional one-step time reversal from tlt_{l} to tl−1t_{l-1} has the closed form

Kl←,x0\displaystyle K_{l}^{\leftarrow,x_{0}} =I+(αl−1−αl)/(1−αl)⋅(ex0−e𝗆)e𝗆⊤,l=1,…,L,\displaystyle=I+(\alpha_{l-1}-\alpha_{l})/(1-\alpha_{l})\cdot(e_{x_{0}}-e_{\mathsf{m}})e_{\mathsf{m}}^{\top},\qquad l=1,\ldots,L,

with kernel qtl,tl−1​(y∣x,x0)=ℙ⁡(Xtl−1=y∣Xtl=x,X0=x0)=ey⊤​Kl←,x0​exq_{t_{l},t_{l-1}}(y\mid x,x_{0})=\mathbb{P}(X_{t_{l-1}}=y\mid X_{t_{l}}=x,X_{0}=x_{0})=e_{y}^{\top}K_{l}^{\leftarrow,x_{0}}e_{x}. Equivalently,

qtl,tl−1​(y∣x,x0)\displaystyle q_{t_{l},t_{l-1}}(y\mid x,x_{0}) ={(αl−1−αl)/(1−αl),x=𝗆,y=x0,(1−αl−1)/(1−αl),x=𝗆,y=𝗆,𝟏{y=x},x≠𝗆,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}(\alpha_{l-1}-\alpha_{l})/(1-\alpha_{l}),&x=\mathsf{m},\ y=x_{0},\\ (1-\alpha_{l-1})/(1-\alpha_{l}),&x=\mathsf{m},\ y=\mathsf{m},\\ \mathbf{1}\{y=x\},&x\neq\mathsf{m},\end{cases}

so an already unmasked token remains fixed while a masked token is either kept masked or revealed as its original clean value. Conditioned on the clean sequence, the true one-step reverse kernel factorizes across coordinates, qtl,tl−1​(𝐱tl−1∣𝐱tl,𝐱0)=∏j=1Nqtl,tl−1​(xtl−1j∣xtlj,x0j)q_{t_{l},t_{l-1}}(\mathbf{x}_{t_{l-1}}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t_{l}},\mathbf{x}_{0})=\prod_{j=1}^{N}q_{t_{l},t_{l-1}}(x_{t_{l-1}}^{j}\mid x_{t_{l}}^{j},x_{0}^{j}), which is the analytic posterior that (2.1) approximates. The same derivation covers the reverse kernel used by the standard masked diffusion sampler in Appendix E.

Appendix G Per-output NFE Breakdown

We record the per-output number of function evaluations (NFE), where one NFE counts one sequence-level masked discrete diffusion forward pass, not one vectorized invocation on a batch. This remains a model-only accounting convention: reward evaluations on completed sequences are reported separately and are not included in NFE. Batching can combine many sequence-level evaluations into one physical call without reducing this count; actual latency also depends on hardware, batch size, memory use, and reward-model latency. Let |⋅||\cdot| denote set cardinality, ssplits_{\mathrm{split}} the number of reverse updates before the best-of-KK split, and [lend,l∗][l_{\mathrm{end}},l^{*}] the guidance window from Appendix H. For update index s∈{0,…,L−1}s\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}, the corresponding reverse state index is l=L−sl=L-s. Define 𝒢={s:lend≤L−s≤l∗}\mathcal{G}=\{s:l_{\mathrm{end}}\leq L-s\leq l^{*}\} as the set of guided updates, with s∈{0,…,L−1}s\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\} throughout. Let the active branch multiplicity be bs=1b_{s}=1 for s<ssplits<s_{\mathrm{split}} and bs=Kb_{s}=K for s≥ssplits\geq s_{\mathrm{split}}, and set S=∑s∈𝒢bsS=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{G}}b_{s}. Under the stated one-head-pass-per-candidate implementation, the per-output model NFE is:

NFE\displaystyle\mathrm{NFE} =|{s:s<ssplit}|+K⋅|{s:ssplit≤s<L}|\displaystyle=|\{s:s<s_{\mathrm{split}}\}|+K\cdot|\{s:s_{\mathrm{split}}\leq s<L\}|
+M⋅|{s:s∈𝒢,s<ssplit}|+K⋅M⋅|{s:s∈𝒢,ssplit≤s<L}|.\displaystyle\quad+M\cdot|\{s:s\in\mathcal{G},\,s<s_{\mathrm{split}}\}|+K\cdot M\cdot|\{s:s\in\mathcal{G},\,s_{\mathrm{split}}\leq s<L\}|. (G.1)

The first line counts the shared base masked discrete diffusion forward pass on 𝐱¯tl\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}} at every update (one pass per update before the split, KK passes per update after). The second line counts the MM candidate prediction-head passes for hh-estimation inside the guidance window, also with the K×K\times multiplier after the split. Equivalently, NFE=∑s=0L−1bs+M​S\mathrm{NFE}=\sum_{s=0}^{L-1}b_{s}+MS. Drawing nhn_{h} completions per candidate leaves this model NFE unchanged when all completions reuse that candidate’s prediction-head probabilities; the executed single-completion sampler uses nh=1n_{h}=1. The corresponding number of scored candidate completions per output is

candidate reward evaluations=nh​M​S.\displaystyle\text{candidate reward evaluations}=n_{h}MS.

If K>1K>1 and a split occurs, terminal ranking requires at most KK additional reward evaluations per output when scores of the final sequences are not cached; candidate-completion scores can be reused only when they score those same final sequences. The number of physical batched reward calls is implementation-dependent and is not this sequence-level evaluation count. Setting K=1K=1 or ssplit=Ls_{\mathrm{split}}=L disables the split and its terminal ranking, recovering the core D-DOIT branch. These counts describe computational work rather than a wall-clock speed guarantee.
