Appendix I Additional Analyses

The main experiments evaluate HepG2 enhancer design, cell-type-specific regulatory DNA design, and protein inverse folding. This appendix collects approximation diagnostics and oracle-transfer analyses; the compute–quality trade-off is discussed in the main text. Matched-time sampling controls are detailed in Sections J.3 and K.5; full diagnostic sweeps appear in Appendix L.

Concentrated but stochastic selection.

At M=8M=8 and ω=8\omega=8, mean ESS is 1.143±0.0021.143\pm 0.002 and the top-weighted candidate is selected on 95.72%95.72\% of guided steps. Soft resampling reaches final guidance reward 5.237±0.0515.237\pm 0.051, versus 5.154±0.0275.154\pm 0.027 for direct argmax in the same diagnostic (Section L.6). Thus selection is near-greedy but not deterministic; low ESS measures local weight concentration, not final-sequence diversity.

Suffix search and nonmonotone progress.

With M=9M=9, K=4K=4, and nh=1n_{h}=1 fixed, moving the split from update 105105 to 00 increases final guidance reward from 5.272±0.0575.272\pm 0.057 to 5.890±0.0285.890\pm 0.028, but raises wall time from 326.4±0.5326.4\pm 0.5 to 793.6±2.2793.6\pm 2.2 seconds per job. Even with 90.38%90.38\% of bases fixed, independent suffix completions differ at 66.1%66.1\% of the remaining positions. Late branching therefore searches a diverse suffix conditional on a fixed prefix; it cannot revise pre-split reveals. Separately, held-out activity of argmax-completed partial states is nonmonotone despite higher final activity than frozen sampling (Section L.7). These completion-proxy scores are distinct from final guidance reward RR and the batch-median Pred-Activity benchmark. The diagnostics characterize practical search trade-offs, not exact reward-tilted sampling.

Appendix J Experimental Details of Regulatory DNA Sequence Design

In this section, we provide the experimental details and additional experimental analysis for the regulatory DNA sequence design task in Section 4.1.

J.1 Dataset and Training Details

Dataset.

We conduct experiments on the HepG2 enhancer corpus from Gosai et al. [24]. The corpus contains ∼700{\sim}700k 200200 bp human enhancer sequences with measured HepG2 activity. We follow the dataset split of Wang et al. [8] so that our evaluation seeds match the DRAKES test partition and our numbers compare against the published DRAKES table.

Reward oracle setup.

We use two Enformer-based oracles [64] from Wang et al. [8]. The two oracles use disjoint chromosome splits of the same corpus. The finetuning oracle provides the reward signal R⁡(𝐱0)R(\mathbf{x}_{0}) during guided sampling. The held-out evaluation oracle scores Pred-Activity at test time. This matches the DRAKES protocol and makes our numbers comparable to the TDS, SMC, CG, and DRAKES results in Wang et al. [8].

Pre-training setup.

D-DOIT operates on a frozen pre-trained masked discrete diffusion model [3]. We do not update its parameters during sampling. We use the public masked discrete diffusion enhancer checkpoint of Wang et al. [8], which the authors pre-train on the ∼700{\sim}700k enhancer corpus.

Sampling setup.

We use the two operating points defined in Section 3.2: D-DOIT-LBOK-S with a small per-step budget plus a late-stage trajectory split, and D-DOIT-Q with a larger inference-time budget for quality. Table 5 lists the exact hyperparameter values per benchmark. All main DRAKES rows use a single A100 80GB GPU and follow the DRAKES evaluation protocol with 640640 sequences per seed. Most rows use 33 random seeds; the re-measured TDS and the adopted D-DOIT-LBOK-S rows use 55 fresh final-test seeds after held-out eval selection. The TDS and D-DOIT-LBOK-S rows are re-measured on an A100-SXM4-80GB GPU; the remaining rows are reported as A100 reruns. Seed identity alone does not guarantee bitwise agreement across hardware or software implementations, so comparisons also require the same checkpoint, sampler, and evaluation protocol. We do not copy numbers from [8], so wall-clock and reward differences against the published table reflect our hardware and seed protocol rather than reporting drift.

J.2 Evaluation Metrics and Baselines

Evaluation metrics.

We use four metrics that cover predicted activity, chromatin accessibility, and sequence naturalness:

  • •

    Predicted activity (Pred-Activity): We use the held-out evaluation reward oracle of [8] to estimate HepG2 enhancer activity for each generated sequence and report the median across the batch following the DRAKES convention. Higher scores indicate more functional sequences.

  • •

    Chromatin accessibility (ATAC-Acc): We use an independent binary classifier trained on ENCODE HepG2 chromatin accessibility data [65] to test whether the designed sequences fall in accessible chromatin regions. This is a key property of active enhancers. Higher accuracy indicates more active sequences.

  • •

    3-mer pearson correlation (3-mer Corr): We compute the Pearson correlation between the 33-mer frequency profile of the generated sequences and that of natural HepG2 enhancers from [24]. Higher correlation indicates that the generated sequences match the overall distribution of natural enhancer sequences.

  • •

    JASPAR motif correlation (JASPAR Corr): We compute the Spearman correlation between the transcription-factor binding motif frequencies of the generated sequences and the natural enhancer reference, scored against the JASPAR motif database [66]. Higher correlation indicates better preservation of regulatory motif structure.

Baselines.

We compare D-DOIT against training-free and training-based methods. Training-free methods steer a frozen pre-trained model at inference time:

  • •

    Pre-trained: the unguided masked discrete diffusion model of [8]; provides the unguided reward and naturalness reference.

  • •

    CG [10]: classifier guidance with discrete gradients; backpropagates through a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation and requires a differentiable reward.

  • •

    SMC and TDS [11]: particle-based guidance with path likelihood ratios. TDS is a strong reported training-free baseline and provides the runtime reference for LBOK-S; its budget is not matched to Q.

  • •

    SVDD-PM [12]: posterior-mean value decoding, using the same frozen MDLM and oracle protocol, with M=416M=416 for similar runtime to Q.

  • •

    Frozen Best-of-NBoNN_{\mathrm{BoN}}: endpoint-only selection over independent unguided samples; NBoN=732N_{\mathrm{BoN}}=732 in the Q wall-clock comparison.

Training-based methods update model parameters:

  • •

    DRAKES [8]: reward finetunes the pre-trained masked discrete diffusion model with a KL regularizer; we treat it as the strongest naturalness-preserving training-based reference.

  • •

    DRAKES w/o KL: removes the KL term to expose the over-optimization risk of unregularized reward maximization.

  • •

    CFG [67]: trains a conditional model from scratch.

J.3 Nearest-neighbor and Endpoint-search Controls

The SVDD-PM comparison uses the same frozen MDLM, guidance Enformer, held-out evaluator, paired seeds 100100–102102, and 640640 final outputs per method and seed. We calibrate its candidate count to M=416M=416 to give a similar wall-clock budget to Q (L=128,M=52,K=8,ssplit=0L=128,M=52,K=8,s_{\mathrm{split}}=0). Pred-Activity is computed as a median within each seed, then summarized by the mean and sample standard deviation across seeds. The measured times are 10.59510.595 and 11.23611.236 seconds per output for Q and SVDD-PM, respectively. Q has higher means on all four metrics; the clearest separation is ATAC-Acc (91.67%91.67\% versus 39.84%39.84\%), while Pred-Activity differs by 0.150.15.

Frozen Best-of-NBoNN_{\mathrm{BoN}} samples independent complete sequences from the same unguided backbone, scores them with the guidance Enformer, and retains the highest-scoring endpoint in each group. A separate held-out Enformer evaluates the retained sequences. Same-A100 calibration gives NBoN=732N_{\mathrm{BoN}}=732, with 10.58710.587 seconds per output compared with Q’s 10.59510.595. Table 6 reports this high-budget comparison independently of the lower-budget diagnostics; Q improves activity, accessibility, and 3-mer correlation, while endpoint selection achieves higher JASPAR correlation (0.9570.957 versus 0.9230.923). This control tests whether spending the same time on more complete unguided endpoints can replace local value-guided transitions. Endpoint selection does not reproduce the activity and accessibility gains, although it better preserves this motif statistic. Reward evaluation is included in the measured wall-clock cost.

Separating model and reward budgets.

Table 7 additionally compares diagnostic settings with five seeds and 640640 outputs per seed. The branched M=9M=9 setting uses 1,9701{,}970 diffusion evaluations per output, close to Best-of-15’s 1,9201{,}920, but incurs substantially more oracle work. Its 1,7771{,}777 reward evaluations include 1,7731{,}773 candidate completions and four terminal scores. Across a 640640-output job, batching combines 1,137,2801{,}137{,}280 scored sequences into 1,2901{,}290 vectorized oracle calls. These counts explain why matching only backbone evaluations does not match wall-clock time.

J.4 Guidance-oracle and Evaluator Robustness

We distinguish two controls, both using five sampling seeds and 640640 sequences per seed. In Table 8, only the guidance oracle changes among Enformer, CNN, and MLP; sampler settings, seeds, output count, held-out Enformer, and biological metrics remain fixed. All three guidance oracles improve held-out activity and accessibility over the frozen model, but the effect size varies with the oracle. Enformer guidance gives the highest activity and accessibility, whereas MLP guidance gives the highest 3-mer correlation in this diagnostic.

In Table 9, we instead rescore the same Enformer-guided and unguided sequences with held-out Enformer, CNN, and MLP predictors. D-DOIT exceeds the frozen model within each evaluator. Because their output scales differ, cross-column score magnitudes are not directly comparable. These controls assess predictor transfer separately from the selected high-budget Q row and do not substitute for experimental biological assays.

J.5 Additional Experimental Analysis

For the experimental results in Table 2, we provide the additional detailed analysis below.

Section 4.1 reports the headline TDS comparisons. We add two pieces of detail here. First, the D-DOIT-LBOK-S vs. TDS gap on ATAC-Acc is +25.0+25.0 percentage points (40.0%→65.0%40.0\%\to 65.0\%), while Pred-Activity is matched (4.564.56 vs. 4.584.58) with lower reported seed variability; this is descriptive, not a variance-test result. The same operating point also lifts ATAC-Acc from 39.9%39.9\% to 65.0%65.0\% over SMC and JASPAR Corr from 0.7560.756 to 0.9480.948 over SMC. Second, high-budget D-DOIT-Q over TDS gives +1.61+1.61 in Pred-Activity, +51.7+51.7 percentage points in ATAC-Acc, +0.077+0.077 in 3-mer Corr, and +0.124+0.124 in JASPAR Corr.

Compared with the training-based DRAKES, D-DOIT-Q achieves higher Pred-Activity (6.196.19 vs. 5.615.61), higher 3-mer Corr (0.8940.894 vs. 0.8870.887), and higher JASPAR Corr (0.9230.923 vs. 0.9110.911) without any backbone update. DRAKES remains higher on ATAC-Acc (92.5%92.5\% vs. 91.7%91.7\%), so we do not claim an all-metric win. The unregularized variant DRAKES w/o KL exposes the cost of training-based reward maximization: it gains +0.83+0.83 in Pred-Activity over DRAKES but loses 0.5800.580 in 3-mer Corr (0.887→0.3070.887\to 0.307) and 0.3540.354 in JASPAR Corr (0.911→0.5570.911\to 0.557). D-DOIT-Q stays near the DRAKES high-naturalness regime. The frozen model supplies candidate proposals without retraining. The exact reference transform reweights its induced distribution; the practical sampler’s temperatures and selection operations change that reference law. Figure 2 plots utility and naturalness for the original benchmark comparison set. The separately time-calibrated SVDD and endpoint controls are reported in Table 6, rather than pooled into a claim of an exhaustive compute–quality frontier. D-DOIT-LBOK-S anchors the practical moderate-budget side of this frontier. D-DOIT-Q occupies the high-utility, high-naturalness corner when inference-time budget is deliberately relaxed, with ATAC-Acc as the remaining gap to DRAKES.

J.6 Held-out Final-test Check for D-DOIT-LBOK-S

We select the DRAKES LBOK-S configuration on eval seeds 42,43,4442,43,44 and report it once on fresh final-test seeds 105,106,107,108,109105,106,107,108,109. The fixed final configuration uses M=9M{=}9, K=4K{=}4, ssplit=105s_{\mathrm{split}}{=}105, ω=3.0\omega{=}3.0, β=0.2\beta{=}0.2, τ=3.0\tau{=}3.0, and γ=1.2\gamma{=}1.2. It exceeds the TDS thresholds on ATAC-Acc, 3-mer Corr, and JASPAR Corr, and has a similar mean Pred-Activity to TDS; no statistical equivalence test is implied.

J.7 Held-out Selection for High-budget D-DOIT-Q

To avoid tuning directly on the final reported seeds, we separate the DRAKES high-budget update into three seed groups. Development seeds 0,1,20,1,2 identify promising sampler families only. Held-out eval seeds 42,43,4442,43,44 select the final high-budget D-DOIT-Q configuration (M=52M{=}52, K=8K{=}8, ssplit=0s_{\mathrm{split}}{=}0, ω=3.0\omega{=}3.0, β=0.2\beta{=}0.2, τ=3.0\tau{=}3.0, γ=1.2\gamma{=}1.2). Final-test seeds 100,101,102100,101,102 are then evaluated once and reported as the held-out final numbers in Table 2.

Appendix K Experimental Details of Cell-type-specific Enhancer Design

In this section, we provide the experimental details and additional experimental analysis for the cell-type-specific enhancer design task in Section 4.2.

K.1 Dataset and Training Details

Dataset.

We use the 200200 bp human enhancer corpus of Chen et al. [25], covering three cell lines: HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH. Data preprocessing follows the regLM protocol of Lal et al. [26], as in Chen et al. [25]. We use the Ctrl-DNA enhancer task only for its data, cell-type-specific reward oracles, and evaluation metrics. The training procedure and backbone architecture come from our own setup, which we describe in the next paragraphs.

Reward oracle setup.

We use the cell-type-specific Enformer-based oracles [64] from Chen et al. [25], which the authors train on the same corpus. Unlike constrained-RL baselines with explicit thresholds and policy retraining, D-DOIT is an inference-time method and accepts a single black-box scalar reward. For target cell line cc and off-target cell lines 𝒞−c\mathcal{C}_{-c}, we set

R⁡(𝐱0)=Rc​(𝐱0)−λ⋅maxc′∈𝒞−c⁡Rc′​(𝐱0),\displaystyle R(\mathbf{x}_{0})=R_{c}(\mathbf{x}_{0})-\lambda\cdot\max_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{-c}}R_{c^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x}_{0}), (K.1)

where each RcR_{c} is the cell-type-specific Enformer oracle of Chen et al. [25]. The max\max over off-targets suppresses the worst case during sampling. The evaluation Δ​R\Delta R averages over off-targets to follow the Ctrl-DNA convention. We sweep λ\lambda on held-out eval seeds disjoint from the final-test seeds. The final high-budget row uses the task-default penalties selected for the Q operating point, and the final low-budget LBOK-S row uses λ=2.0\lambda=2.0 selected by the low-budget eval sweep.

Pre-training setup.

We train a new masked discrete diffusion model [3] on the Ctrl-DNA enhancer corpus. The HyenaDNA backbone used by Chen et al. [25] is autoregressive and does not fit our discrete hh-transform. D-DOIT operates on this frozen model without updating its parameters during sampling. The same checkpoint serves all three cell lines and both operating points.

Sampling setup.

We use the two operating points from Section 3.2. Table 5 lists the exact hyperparameter values per benchmark. For the D-DOIT Ctrl-DNA rows, we choose fixed configs on eval seeds 42,43,4442,43,44 and report final-test seeds 100,101,102,103,104100,101,102,103,104. We use 55 random seeds with batch size 256256 per seed and run a separate set for each of the three target cell lines. Pre-trained, CG, SMC, and TDS are the rerun training-free comparison rows. Other baselines come from the reported results in Chen et al. [25] Table 1 under the 55-seed, δ=0.5\delta=0.5 setting.

K.2 Evaluation Metrics and Baselines

Evaluation metrics.

We use three metrics that cover cell-type specificity, motif structure, and set-level diversity:

  • •

    Cell-specific reward difference (Δ​R\Delta R): We compute the difference between the target-cell oracle score and the average of the off-target oracle scores following the Ctrl-DNA convention. Higher scores indicate stronger cell-type specificity.

  • •

    Motif correlation (Motif Corr): We compute the Pearson correlation between the transcription-factor binding-site frequencies of the generated sequences and the cell-type-specific natural enhancer set from [25] (top half by target activity, bottom half by off-target activity). Higher correlation indicates that the generated sequences match the regulatory grammar of natural cell-specific enhancers.

  • •

    Set-level diversity (Diversity): We compute the Shannon entropy across the generated sequence set with the official Ctrl-DNA evaluation script [25]. Higher entropy indicates that the sampler does not collapse onto a small set of high-reward sequences.

Δ​R\Delta R and Motif Corr appear in Table 3. Diversity appears in Figure 3. We omit Median because [25] mentions it in text but does not report numerical values.

Baselines.

We compare D-DOIT against the baselines from Chen et al. [25] and the same training-free guidance methods as in Section J.2:

  • •

    Pre-trained, CG [10], SMC, TDS [11]: training-free inference-time methods on the same frozen masked discrete diffusion model. These share the frozen backbone with D-DOIT. Frozen Best-of-708 additionally provides the same-A100 endpoint-search control at Q’s measured time budget.

  • •

    regLM [26]: supervised generative baseline that the authors train on the cell-type-specific enhancer corpus.

  • •

    PPO, TACO, PPO-Lagrangian [25]: RL-based methods that retrain the generator against the specificity reward.

  • •

    AdaLead, PEX, BO, CMA-ES [25]: directed-evolution methods that search the sequence space directly without any generative backbone.

K.3 Training-free Baseline Tuning Screen

To check that the Ctrl-DNA training-free baselines are not weak only because of arbitrary default hyperparameters, we run a bounded seed-42 screen for CG, SMC, and TDS on HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH. Table 12 summarizes all 13 screened configurations at the family level and names the selected follow-up configuration for each baseline family. Across this screen, CG remains a high-motif, near-zero-reward baseline; SMC obtains only small reward movement and degrades motif/diversity; and TDS remains weak on the composite specificity reward. Because this is a one-seed screen rather than a final-test protocol, we use it as baseline-tuning provenance instead of replacing the main-table baseline rows reported above.

K.4 Additional Experimental Analysis

For the experimental results in Table 3, we provide the additional detailed analysis below.

Table 3 records positive mean specificity for the two D-DOIT configurations relative to the originally reported CG, SMC, and TDS rows. The time-calibrated endpoint control additionally attains positive specificity, with mean Δ​R=0.108\Delta R=0.108. Compared with TDS, D-DOIT-LBOK-S improves Δ​R\Delta R from 0.0020.002 to 0.0330.033 and improves Motif Corr from 0.5730.573 to 0.6480.648, at about 0.94×0.94\times the rerun TDS wall-clock in the Ctrl-DNA timing logs. CG fails to move the specificity reward at all (Δ​R≈0\Delta R\approx 0, indistinguishable from Pre-trained), and SMC sits at Δ​R=0.000\Delta R=0.000 with Motif Corr 0.5870.587. Q reaches Δ​R=0.119±0.063\Delta R=0.119\pm 0.063 and Motif Corr 0.498±0.0700.498\pm 0.070. Its 5.435.43 seconds per output is close to Frozen Best-of-708’s 5.515.51 on the same A100. The small mean advantage over endpoint selection is not claimed statistically significant. Table 13 provides the per-cell breakdown for the original guidance comparisons.

Compared with the remaining training-based baselines, D-DOIT-Q stays behind regLM on Δ​R\Delta R (0.1190.119 vs. 0.160.16). Because regLM uses a different generative backbone and training procedure, this gap does not isolate the effect of inference-time adaptation. On Motif Corr, D-DOIT-Q at 0.4980.498 exceeds every remaining training-based and evolutionary baseline (PPO-Lagrangian 0.420.42, AdaLead 0.360.36). These means describe motif preservation at the reported specificity levels; they do not identify which mechanism caused the difference. Pre-trained has high Motif Corr (0.9370.937) at Δ​R≈0\Delta R\approx 0, providing an unguided naturalness reference rather than a mathematical ceiling. LBOK-S has higher Motif Corr (0.6480.648) than Q and Frozen Best-of-708, while achieving lower specificity. D-DOIT-Q (0.4980.498) trades motif fidelity for higher Δ​R\Delta R, so we use it as the high-specificity operating point rather than a motif-preserving one.

Figure 3 compares diversity and specificity within the original guidance baseline set; the endpoint control’s reward and motif scores are compared separately in Table 3. SMC and TDS gain little Δ​R\Delta R and collapse Shannon entropy to ≈1.5\approx 1.5. D-DOIT-Q occupies the high-Δ​R\Delta R, high-diversity region across all three cell lines. Table 13 reports the per-cell breakdown of Δ​R\Delta R, Motif Corr, and Diversity.

The headline averages in Table 3 are the cross-cell means of these rows. Both D-DOIT operating points achieve their largest Δ​R\Delta R on K562, consistent with K562 carrying the largest reward headroom in the Ctrl-DNA setup, with smaller positive gains on HepG2 and SK-N-SH. D-DOIT-LBOK-S wins on Motif Corr for every cell line among training-free methods that move the reward. Both D-DOIT operating points keep Diversity high (≈1.98\approx 1.98) on all three cells. SMC and TDS drop to ≈1.5\approx 1.5.

The final Ctrl-DNA Q operating point uses M=52M=52, K=20K=20, and ssplit=64s_{\mathrm{split}}=64, whereas DRAKES Q uses M=52M=52, K=8K=8, and ssplit=0s_{\mathrm{split}}=0. A preceding Ctrl-DNA eval sweep also considered M=8,K=20,ssplit=64M=8,K=20,s_{\mathrm{split}}=64, which obtained config-level Δ​R=0.117\Delta R=0.117, and a M=32,K=8,ssplit=0M=32,K=8,s_{\mathrm{split}}=0 setting with Δ​R=0.105\Delta R=0.105 at roughly three times the runtime. These exploratory settings differ from the final Q comparison and vary several parameters together. They illustrate alternative budget allocations, not an isolated causal effect of branching. The endpoint control shows that final selection alone already obtains much of the mean specificity gain under the calibrated budget.

K.5 Wall-clock-matched Endpoint Control

Frozen Best-of-708 generates complete unguided sequences from the frozen backbone and retains the best reward-scored endpoint in each group. We calibrate its group size on the same A100 used for Q (L=128,M=52,K=20,ssplit=64L=128,M=52,K=20,s_{\mathrm{split}}=64). At 5.515.51 versus 5.435.43 seconds per output, the methods give specificity 0.108±0.02810.108\pm 0.0281 versus 0.119±0.0630.119\pm 0.063, and Motif Corr 0.490±0.1650.490\pm 0.165 versus 0.498±0.0700.498\pm 0.070. The means favor Q slightly, but the differences are modest and are not interpreted as statistically significant. Training-based rows remain cross-backbone references, separate from this inference-time comparison.

Appendix L Ablation Study

We conduct ablation studies on the DRAKES HepG2 enhancer task to understand the behavior of D-DOIT. We examine the guidance window l∗l^{*}, guidance strength ω\omega and effective sample size (ESS), proposal and completion temperatures τ,γ\tau,\gamma, and candidate budget MM. We also study completion count, direct-versus-rollout value estimates, soft-versus-argmax selection, split position, and reward trajectories (Tables 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21). The window, strength, temperature, and candidate-budget sweeps use a single held-out seed unless noted otherwise; the additional diagnostics state their sampling protocols separately. Final guidance reward RR is scored by the sampling oracle and is distinct from held-out Pred-Activity. Completion-proxy trajectories use the held-out evaluator but average scores of completed partial states rather than the benchmark’s within-seed batch median. We re-run the best γ\gamma-sweep configuration across the 33 main evaluation seeds and report it in Table 15. These studies show how D-DOIT balances reward optimization, sequence naturalness, and computational cost.

The candidate-budget sweep shows that increasing MM mainly improves functional utility, while naturalness metrics remain comparatively stable. The table surfaces three consequential design choices: the guidance window l∗l^{*} exhibits a phase transition for naturalness; the completion temperature γ\gamma controls prediction-head completion quality; and the candidate budget MM controls utility.

Runtime analysis.

Section 4.4 reports the runtime comparison and its measurement conditions. The runtime pattern follows the NFE accounting in Appendix G: larger MM and earlier best-of-KK splitting increase candidate-state evaluations and oracle-scored completions. Increasing nhn_{h} also increases completion scoring, as quantified in Table 16. LBOK-S is the lower-budget operating point, whereas Q deliberately trades greater recurring inference cost for quality; neither setting implies cost dominance over training-based methods.

L.1 Effect of Guidance Window l∗l^{*}

We study the effect of the guidance window l∗l^{*}, the highest reverse-time index where Doob’s hh-transform is active in the discrete sampler. A smaller l∗l^{*} saves (L−l∗)⋅M(L-l^{*})\cdot M neural-function evaluations per sequence but omits guidance at more heavily masked states, where limited revealed context may affect the prediction-head proxy. Figure 4 reports the four DRAKES metrics as we sweep l∗∈{10,20,…,128}l^{*}\in\{10,20,\ldots,128\}.

The results show a phase-transition-like behavior in naturalness. All configurations with l∗≤50l^{*}\leq 50 produce negative 3-mer Pearson correlations. A sharp jump occurs between l∗=96l^{*}{=}96 (3-mer =0.21=0.21) and l∗=112l^{*}{=}112 (0.650.65). At l∗=128l^{*}{=}128, 3-mer reaches 0.8940.894, a 14×14\times improvement over l∗=64l^{*}{=}64. Utility metrics improve across the same range without a sharp transition. In this sweep, broad guidance windows are associated with better global sequence-composition statistics; this observation does not isolate a causal mechanism or establish a requirement for other rewards. Utility metrics, in contrast, recover from a narrower window. We use l∗=128l^{*}{=}128 as the default setting.

L.2 Effect of Guidance Strength ω\omega and ESS Collapse

We study the effect of the guidance strength ω\omega in (3.7). A larger ω\omega sharpens the transformed transition toward high-reward candidates. A smaller ω\omega preserves more of the pre-trained kernel.

Figure 5 reports the per-step Effective Sample Size (ESS) of the candidate weights and the fraction of steps where ESS collapses below M/4M/4. The results show that ESS collapses to near 11 at ω≥4\omega\geq 4. 95%95\% of guided steps have ESS <M/4<M/4 at ω=4\omega{=}4, and 100%100\% at ω≥16\omega\geq 16. A direct mechanism for concentration is reward-range amplification: ω=4\omega{=}4 amplifies a candidate reward range of ≈3\approx 3 nats to ≥12\geq 12 nats and saturates the softmax. High-quality results remain achievable despite this collapse when proposal-level diversity (via τ\tau) still places a strong candidate in the pool. This motivates joint tuning of ω\omega and τ\tau, but does not imply that larger τ\tau recovers importance-weight accuracy. The concentration depends on the reward distribution and ω/β\omega/\beta, so these diagnostic thresholds cannot be transferred unchanged to other configurations.

L.3 Effect of Proposal and Completion Temperatures τ,γ\tau,\gamma

We then study the joint effect of the proposal temperature τ\tau in (3.6) and the completion temperature γ\gamma in (3.3). A larger τ\tau flattens the proposal and produces more diverse candidates. A smaller γ\gamma sharpens the prediction-head completion toward the model mode. Figure 6 reports the four DRAKES metrics across the joint sweep at M=32M{=}32.

The results show a clear separation of roles. Functional activity peaks at higher proposal diversity. Marginal analysis shows Pred-Activity improves from 3.893.89 at τ=2.5\tau{=}2.5 to 4.074.07 at τ=5.0\tau{=}5.0, and ATAC-Acc from 53.7%53.7\% to 69.4%69.4\%. Naturalness peaks at sharper prediction-head completions. Reducing γ\gamma from 1.21.2 to 0.60.6 improves averaged 3-mer Corr from 0.8460.846 to 0.9050.905. At the strongest γ\gamma-sweep configuration (M=32M{=}32, τ=3.0\tau{=}3.0, γ=0.6\gamma{=}0.6), 3-mer Corr reaches 0.949±0.0060.949\pm 0.006 across 33 seeds, above DRAKES at 0.8870.887. This sweep identifies the naturalness-preserving region. The final held-out DRAKES Q row in Table 2 uses a larger eval-selected inference budget and trades some naturalness for much higher Pred-Activity and ATAC-Acc while remaining above the DRAKES 3-mer and JASPAR targets. Naturalness metrics saturate around τ=3.5\tau{=}3.5–4.04.0, suggesting a trade-off between naturalness and accessibility at extreme proposal temperatures. We use τ=3.0\tau{=}3.0 and γ=0.6\gamma{=}0.6 as the ablation default for naturalness-preserving sweeps.

L.4 Effect of Candidate Budget MM

We study the effect of the Monte Carlo candidate budget MM. The candidate count controls per-step work and coverage of possible next states. This sweep measures quality changes, not kernel error or convergence to the original tilted distribution. Figure 7 reports the four DRAKES metrics across M∈{8,16,32}M\in\{8,16,32\}.

The results show that fewer candidates reduce functional utility but leave sequence naturalness almost unchanged. Reducing MM from 3232 to 88 drops Pred-Activity by 31%31\% and ATAC-Acc by 29%29\%. 3-mer Corr drops by 9%9\% and JASPAR Corr by less than 1%1\%. The temperatures and the guidance window drive naturalness. A larger candidate count gives more direct help to utility. M=32M{=}32 provides a strong per-step default within the ablation sweep. The final held-out DRAKES Q row uses a larger budget, M=52M{=}52 with K=8K{=}8, for the no-budget-limit quality comparison in Table 2.

L.5 Completion Count and Matched-state Proxy Diagnostics

Completion count nhn_{h} and candidate count MM address different aspects of sampling: MM controls candidate-state coverage, whereas nhn_{h} controls the number of prediction-head completions averaged for each candidate in (3.5). We reserve NN for sequence length. Table 16 reports the full sampler with five seeds and 3,2003{,}200 sequences per setting. Increasing nhn_{h} from 11 to 22 raises final guidance reward by 0.4920.492, at 41%41\% additional wall time; nh=3n_{h}=3 raises reward by 0.7060.706, at 81%81\% additional wall time. We retain nh=1n_{h}=1 as the practical compute–quality default. More completions reduce sampling variance for the head expectation, but do not remove its factorization or temperature mismatch with sequential rollouts. The completion-count sweep therefore measures a practical quality–cost trade-off while retaining the same factorized head approximation.

To examine the completion law, we save 640640 matched partial states at each of three stages from 128128 DRAKES HepG2 source trajectories per seed over five seeds. From each state, we independently generate 3232 direct prediction-head completions and 3232 sequential reverse-process continuations. For each route, we compute the hh-value corresponding to each completion’s reward and average these values over the 3232 completions. Table 17 summarizes the pooled distributions of these per-state averages. The fixed-base fraction is the percentage of nucleotides already revealed in the partial state. W1 is Wasserstein-1 distance; KS is the maximum absolute difference between the two empirical cumulative distribution functions, not a significance-test result.

The pooled means are similar, while W1 increases from 0.0600.060 at 0.78%0.78\% fixed bases to 0.1240.124 at 66.34%66.34\%. KS remains between 0.0450.045 and 0.0580.058. Thus the direct head gives a useful low-cost marginal approximation in this diagnostic, with residual distributional shift that grows across the sampled stages. These pooled summaries do not imply equality of the conditional completion laws or exact sampling from the reward-tilted target.

L.6 Soft Selection versus Argmax

Table 18 compares soft selection in (3.7) with direct argmax using M=8M=8, τ=3\tau=3, K=4K=4, and β=0.2\beta=0.2, over five seeds and 3,2003{,}200 sequences per setting. This diagnostic is separate from the high-budget Q operating point. As ω\omega rises from 11 to 88, mean ESS falls from 1.8771.877 to 1.1431.143 and top-candidate selection rises from 77.53%77.53\% to 95.72%95.72\%. At ω=1\omega=1, soft selection has lower final guidance reward than argmax (4.894±0.0554.894\pm 0.055 versus 5.154±0.0275.154\pm 0.027); at ω=8\omega=8, it has higher reward (5.237±0.0515.237\pm 0.051). The behavior is therefore close to stochastic best-of-MM selection, rather than broad resampling, but not identical to argmax. The remaining 4.28%4.28\% non-top selections at ω=8\omega=8 can change subsequent states and candidate pools. Low ESS describes local weight concentration, not final-sequence diversity or target-distribution accuracy.

L.7 Split Time and Reward Trajectories

Earlier branching improves reward at greater cost.

Table 19 varies only ssplits_{\mathrm{split}}, keeping M=9M=9, K=4K=4, and nh=1n_{h}=1 fixed. Splitting at update 00 gives final guidance reward 5.890±0.0285.890\pm 0.028 and a best-of-44 gain of 1.605±0.0191.605\pm 0.019; splitting at update 105105 gives 5.272±0.0575.272\pm 0.057 and 0.959±0.0200.959\pm 0.020, respectively. The earlier split costs 793.6±2.2793.6\pm 2.2 seconds per job, compared with 326.4±0.5326.4\pm 0.5 seconds for the late split. Late branching retains a useful selection gain while sharing more of the trajectory computation, but it cannot revise tokens already fixed before the split.

Diversity remains in the unresolved suffix.

For saved partial states from the frozen reverse process, we sample 3232 independent suffix completions and compute pairwise Hamming distance only on positions that were still masked (Table 20). The distance is 0.710±0.0100.710\pm 0.010 with 25.43%25.43\% of bases fixed, and remains 0.661±0.0110.661\pm 0.011 with 90.38%90.38\% fixed. These results demonstrate substantial suffix diversity conditional on a shared prefix, not determinism of early reveals. Late best-of-KK exploits this remaining search space; the complete D-DOIT–TDS comparison does not isolate branching’s contribution.

Completion-proxy progress is nonmonotone.

Table 21 scores partial states after filling masked positions with the frozen model’s deterministic argmax predictions. The held-out Enformer scores are averaged over 640640 sequences per seed and then over five seeds. They are neither guidance reward RR nor the batch-median Pred-Activity metric. D-DOIT’s completion-proxy score rises from 2.0672.067 at update 11 to 2.3282.328 at update 3232, falls to 1.7581.758 at update 9696, and reaches 3.6703.670 at update 128128; frozen sampling declines from 2.0532.053 to 0.3710.371. This trajectory shows higher endpoint activity without monotone intermediate progress. An argmax-completion score is not the rollout hh-function or a guarantee about future reward.

From update 3232 onward, the argmax-completed D-DOIT sequences are 100%100\% unique, and their mean pairwise Hamming distance increases from 0.7260.726 to 0.7490.749. This diversity measure concerns completed sequences across the sample batch, unlike the remaining-position conditional diversity above. The observed late-stage reward improvement is therefore compatible with maintained diversity in this diagnostic, rather than implying that guidance universally preserves diversity.

Appendix M Experimental Details of Protein Inverse Folding

Protein inverse folding tests amino-acid sequence design conditional on a target backbone, complementing the regulatory DNA experiments, and the full cross-method comparison, including all metrics and seed-level SDs, is in Table 22. We follow the protein inverse-folding protocol of DRAKES [8], using the same reward oracle and evaluation metrics. D-DOIT guides the frozen conditional generator through reward-value queries without updating its parameters.

Protocol and aggregation.

We evaluate all 1212 test protein backbones with three independent sampling seeds and generate 128128 sequences per backbone and seed. The configuration M=52M=52, K=8K=8, and nh=1n_{h}=1 (one completion per candidate) is fixed before test-set evaluation, with no tuning after inspecting test results. Each metric is computed separately for each seed under the DRAKES protocol; D-DOIT entries report the mean and sample standard deviation across those three seed-level metrics. The uncertainty describes sampling-seed variation, not variation across sequences or backbones.

Metrics.

Pred-ddG is the predicted stability score, with higher values preferred under the benchmark’s sign convention. We report its median and the percentage of sequences with predicted ddG greater than zero. Structural fidelity is measured by self-consistency RMSD (scRMSD), comparing the predicted structure of a generated sequence with its target backbone; we report the median in Å and the percentage below 22 Å. Joint success requires both positive predicted ddG and scRMSD below 22 Å. These are predictor-based measures rather than experimental stability or folding measurements.

Results and comparison boundary.

D-DOIT achieves the highest median Pred-ddG (0.870±0.0460.870\pm 0.046), ddG-positive fraction (74.8±3.1%74.8\pm 3.1\%), and joint success (68.1±3.5%68.1\pm 3.5\%) among the six methods. Joint success exceeds the published SMC and TDS means by 4.54.5 and 5.25.2 percentage points, respectively. TDS retains better structural fidelity: median scRMSD is 0.8340.834 Å versus 0.8720.872 Å, and the fraction below 22 Å is 94.4%94.4\% versus 92.5%92.5\%. All non-D-DOIT entries are taken directly from DRAKES Table 2 and were not rerun in this comparison; their reported uncertainties are retained. The shared benchmark oracle and metrics permit a literature comparison, not a matched-compute or matched-implementation claim. The results extend the computational evaluation to protein sequence design; they do not establish experimentally measured stability or folding.
